title: The Best Years of Our Lives: A triumph by William Wyler

commenti.body:
I love this movie and watch it a few times a year. I believe it was one of the first to show returning soldiers and their actual realities and NOT the fabricated 'for Hollywood' sentimentalities and perfection where everyone returned home without a drinking problem, with their bodies intact, right back to their old jobs. It dealt with the family side of the equation too - how to handle the men being home after so many years away and the adjustment, while recognizing that time and experience meant they were different on return. Marie the three-week wife of Fred even had a line on that - 'we're right back where we started just as if the war had never happened."

Glad you finally watched it, I always wish the story hadn't ended where it did (though clearly it had to) - I wanted to know what Fred got up to with his new job and how things ended up with Peggy. That to me is usually the sign of a well written story.

Yes, I am glad I watched it as well! Given the significance of that air field scene and the meaning of the job, I think it's fair to say that Fred did succeed. As for how things ended up with Peggy, I am confident things did work out with the couple. This film was quite optimistic but it's intelligent enough not to write anything in stone.

Amazing film that everyone should see once before they pass away.

Also it’s William Wyler the lost versatile director in film history? He’s touched on just about every genre imaginable and excelled

> I don't want to spoil my favorite scene but it's with Dana Andrews. At one point in the film, he visits a particular place. He dies there. No, I am not giving anything away but I am telling you what occured. Everything that occurs in that scene seems rather mundane but it means so much to Andrews and with actions and little dialogue, that scene becomes one of the most compelling in cinema history.

It’s unfortunate that Dana Andrews didn’t get an Oscar nomination that year because if you ask me he had the best performance in the film
He is the sort of director that doesn't exist anymore, a great craftsman that seemed  to flourish in just about any genre.
Dana Andrews was a master of understatement. He never once fell into the trap of scenery chewing,  he always executed his performances easily and naturally. That man was ahead of his time.

He had one of filmographies of the 40s I mean just look at it Laura,The Best Years of Our Lives,The Ox-Bow Incident,Boomerang,State Fair,Ball of Fire,Fallen Angel, and A Walk in the Sun. At least 4 of them are in the national film registry which is tied with Bogart for most of that decade

The scene where Fredric March and Myrna Loy first see each other upon his return home — man. I’ve seen this movie a half-dozen times now, and that one scene hits harder and harder, the older that I get.  

First-rate acting, direction, writing, even the music - this is a perfect movie. There’s no room for improvement; not that I can see, anyway.
Ox-Bow is one of my favorite Westerns! I think it's fair to say that it was at least twenty years ahead of it's time because it emphasized the senseless violence of the lawless West.
I agree. Best Years does everything right.

Robert Wise was another versatile director. He made horror films like The Haunting (one of my horror favs), science fiction like the Andromeda Strain, Day the Earth Stood Still, Star Trek 1, musicals like West Side Story and Sound of Music, usual collection of thrillers, war movies and westerns, etc

>musicals like West Side Story and Sound of Music

directing these two in the same decade is insane
[removed]

Indeed, "The Best Years of Our Lives" is a subtle and masterful piece of cinema. Wyler's ability to present deep and complex emotions in such an effortless yet profound manner is amazing. The way you describe the scene with Dana Andrews perfectly encapsulates the essence of the film. It's intriguing how the film taps into the universal human experience of struggle and transition, whether it's a war vet trying to reintegrate into society or any of us navigating the highs and lows of life. I indeed share your sentiment that this film will continue to hold relevance for many years to come.

Making a film about war without actually showing the war is a daring and difficult task. How do others feel about "The Best Years of Our Lives" presenting the post-war period and societal adjustment in America? Do you think it successfully portrays the diverse emotional landscapes of its characters? What other films do you think have done justice to this theme?
Tutored by the great Val Lewton!

I think it really brought to the forefront the very real problem of what they then called "Shell Shock" and what we now call PTSD after an often savage experience in WW2.   Beyond that I don't know, but that's what I most admire about the film.
A lot of directors from that era were incredibly versatile: Robert Wise (already mentioned), Howard Hawks, Billy Wilder, Raoul Walsh, King Vider, Henry King, to name a few. Very good craftsmen.

Eh, let's not gild the lily. One can go "big," without necessarily "chewing the scenery,"  
e.g., Katharine Hepburn, James Stewart, Barbra Stanwyck, etc. Andrews was a perfectly serviceable actor, no more no less. His movies were better than his talent.

I think he was way more than serviceable, he transmitted a sort of  intensity by being subtle. In Where The Sidewalk Ends,  my favorite moment of his performance is when he discovers that he killed a man. The calm, the concern, and then the steady build to full blown panic. I honest to God think that that acting is better than entire performances from other actors. He was understated and highly effective.
Would you put Ang Lee and/or Peter Weir in that same category?
And from a slightly later era, Sidney Lumet.

Great film.

Great performance by non-actor Harold Russell.
The Archers
Not only shellshock but how to live with a physical impairment in an ableist society.

I love how you laid out all your reasons for not wanting to watch it… and then, holy hell, this is incredible!

It’s a fantastic movie that I can’t recommend enough.
Yeah, I suppose both could fit in that category. Also, William Friedkin who recently passed away.
Hawks, Wilder, and even Walsh I would consider to be auteurs. They were not visual poets like John Ford but they did have specific views of reality.
[removed]
He made plenty of films during the classic era Hollywood so he counts

> Andrews was a perfectly serviceable actor, no more no less. His movies were better than his talent.

Nah he was a phenomenal actor that improved the movies he was in
Thank you the poster from above is really underselling Dana
I love P & P but I think they were undoubtedly straight-up auteurs (writer-producer-directors).
Can you explain how that is different to being versatile directors, as was being discussed?

I guess the difference is that someone like William Wyler or Sidney Lumet or Ang Lee starts with someone else's script and then translates that script into a film, whereas Powell & Pressburger started with writing their own scripts.

One could also argue, in an auteurist way, that Powell & Pressburger have consistent themes/stylistic elements running throughout all their films, as diverse as they are. Whereas someone who didn't know that, say, *Sense and Sensibility* and *Hulk* were both directed by Ang Lee wouldn't necessarily think they shared a director.

Re: William Wyler, consider just how different *The Best Years of Our Lives* is from his other Best Picture winner, *Ben-Hur*, and how different both films are from *Roman Holiday*.
I think the fact that Wilder, who began as a screenwriter, eventually became a director-producer-screenwriter (IE on *The Apartment*) really supports that.
Thanks for the explanation. I guess I was thinking that something like The Red Shoes is so different to A Matter of Life and Death in terms of directing, but I can see your point more about genres.

Wrote my MA dissertation about Powell & Pressburger, believe it or not.

I think there is a *Best Years of Our Lives* connection: both it and *A Canterbury Tale* feature an American serviceman basically playing himself in a great performance.
Interesting, thanks!
Cukor’s *I’ll Be Seeing You* (1944) also features a returned soldier who is experiencing PTSD and panic attacks for anyone who wants to check out how other contemporary films handled it.
Never heard it but I will check it out. You can rarely go wrong with Cukor.

It’s odd, I haven’t seen it in a long time, and some listings of it don’t mention Cukor at all. Letterboxd says it was co-directed by Cukor and Dieterle. IMDB lists Cukor as an uncredited director. So, who knows how much input he really had, but it’s a decent Christmas drama.

I realize I am a little late to the party. However, I wanted to share that I rewatched *The Best Years of Our Lives* after reading your wonderful post about this great film. I echo your feelings that one can relate to the characters even without being a veteran. Adapting to a society in transition can have a complex and difficult emotional impact on any individual. After experiencing personal trauma, these feelings may be intensified. The film has so many fascinating themes. One can analyze its ideas of love and marriage, self-identity, social alienation, psychological trauma, societal responsibility, etc.

Thank you again for sharing your insights on this tremendous film!
You're welcome!
